title: An Indian Immigrant's Son Launches to the Space Station on Monday. He Spent a Year in India Vaccinating Children Against Polio.
excerpt: NASA astronaut Anil Menon — born to a Kerala-origin father and a Ukrainian mother in Minneapolis — lifts off aboard Soyuz MS-29 on July 14 for an eight-month mission. He is a Harvard neuroscientist, Stanford physician, former SpaceX flight surgeon, and the latest in a growing line of Indian-origin Americans reaching orbit.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Anil Menon, a NASA astronaut, launches to the ISS on July 14 for an eight-month mission.
  • Menon has a unique background as a son of Indian and Ukrainian immigrants.
  • He previously worked on polio vaccination efforts in India, connecting him to his heritage.
  • Menon is part of a growing lineage of Indian-origin astronauts, including Kalpana Chawla and Sunita Williams.
  • His wife, Anna Menon, is also a NASA astronaut, making them a rare married astronaut pair.
Anil Menon's Journey to Space

On Monday morning, a colonel in the United States Space Force with roots that trace to Kerala will climb into a Soyuz spacecraft at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan and leave the planet. Dr. Anil Madhavan Samoilenko Menon — NASA astronaut, emergency medicine physician, mechanical engineer, and the former medical director of SpaceX — is scheduled to launch aboard Soyuz MS-29 at 10:47 AM Eastern Time on July 14. He will dock with the International Space Station roughly three hours later, beginning an eight-month mission as a flight engineer for Expeditions 74 and 75. It will be his first spaceflight. He will launch alongside two Russian crew members: commander Pyotr Dubrov and flight engineer Anna Kikina, both of Roscosmos. Their callsign is Tigris. For the Indian diaspora, Menon's mission carries a weight that extends beyond the technical. He is the latest in a line of Indian-origin astronauts — after Kalpana Chawla, Sunita Williams, and Raja Chari — to reach orbit. But his path to the launchpad is uniquely Indian-American, shaped by the immigrant experience in ways that are hard to miss. ## The Kerala Thread ![Kalpana Chawla — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9c/Kalpana_Chawla%2C_NASA_photo_portrait_in_orange_suit.jpg) Menon was born on October 15, 1976, in Minneapolis, Minnesota, to an Indian father with roots in Kerala and a Ukrainian mother. The name Madhavan — his middle name — hints at the lineage. He grew up in the American Midwest, but his connection to India was not abstract. After graduating from Harvard University with a degree in neurobiology, Menon spent a year in India as a Rotary Ambassadorial Scholar, working on polio vaccination efforts. It was a formative experience — the kind of immersion that connects second-generation immigrants to the country their parents left. He saw the India that most NRIs know only from family visits: its public health infrastructure, its scale, its contradictions. > **"He graduated with the 23rd astronaut class — known as "the Flies" — in 2024."** He went on to Stanford University, where he earned a master's degree in mechanical engineering and a medical degree. He trained in emergency and aerospace medicine at Stanford and the University of Texas Medical Branch. ## From Earthquake Rubble to the Launchpad Menon's career before NASA reads like a humanitarian case file. He was a first responder during the 2010 Haiti earthquake, the 2011 Reno Air Show crash, and the 2015 Nepal earthquake — an event that hit close to home for the South Asian community. He served in the US Air Force, deploying to Afghanistan and assisting in high-altitude medical rescue operations on Mount Everest. He then joined SpaceX as its first flight surgeon, where he helped build the medical organisation that supported the company's human spaceflight programme. He was part of the team that launched the first crewed Dragon spacecraft on NASA's SpaceX Demo-2 mission in 2020. NASA selected Menon as an astronaut candidate in 2021. He graduated with the 23rd astronaut class — known as "the Flies" — in 2024. ![Sunita Williams — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Sunita_Williams_in_2018.jpg/3840px-Sunita_Williams_in_2018.jpg) ## A Family in Orbit There is a second layer to Menon's story that makes it singular in space history. His wife, Anna Menon, is also a NASA astronaut. She was a SpaceX employee when she flew aboard the Polaris Dawn mission with Jared Isaacman in 2024 — the first private mission to include an extravehicular activity. She was later selected into NASA's astronaut corps. Isaacman, her former mission commander, is now the NASA Administrator. The connections within the American space community are small enough that the professional and personal threads wind together tightly. When Menon launches on Monday, the couple will join the handful of married astronaut pairs in NASA's history. Whether their missions eventually overlap aboard the station remains to be seen.

## What He Will Do Up There Menon will spend approximately 240 days aboard the ISS, conducting scientific research and technology demonstrations designed to advance human space exploration. As a physician-astronaut, his medical expertise will be an asset for the crew's health maintenance programme — a particular concern during long-duration missions. ![Anna Menon — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/NASA_astronaut_candidate_Anna_Menon_%28jsc2025e074865%29.jpg/3840px-NASA_astronaut_candidate_Anna_Menon_%28jsc2025e074865%29.jpg) The Soyuz MS-29 mission marks the return of crewed Soyuz launches from Baikonur's Site 31/6, which was damaged during a launch incident in November 2025 when a mobile service platform came loose. The pad was repaired and successfully tested with an uncrewed resupply mission in March. "Then I knew the launchpad was working and functional after the issues they had before," Menon told NASASpaceFlight.com. "That's when I felt like I was at the peak of the roller coaster, and you're just tipping over, and it was that moment of excitement and thrill that it was coming no matter what." ## The Diaspora Moment India's own Gaganyaan human spaceflight programme is preparing to send Indian astronauts to space — four were introduced by Prime Minister Modi at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre. Last year, Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla became the first Indian aboard the ISS through the Axiom Mission 4 programme. Menon's mission sits at the intersection of these trajectories: the American space programme that gave Indian immigrants' children a path to orbit, and the Indian programme that is now building its own. He carries both flags, whether he is conscious of it or not — the Kerala connection in his name, the Stanford degree in his credentials, the year he spent in Indian villages with a vaccine in his hand.
